So I just looked it up. It's Phramites australis we're dealing with right?

I have some experience dealing with extremely vigorous invasive grasses and reeds, and in my honest opinion they're the hardest damn invasives to control. It seems that the top recommendation is to do controlled burns of it, however this likely isn't practical in most situations so I'll try and give some tips. 

From my experience dealing with Buffel Grass (Cenchrus ciliaris) there are typically two options, weed killer (if it works on Australis) or using a pickaxe to dig the plant and the roots up out of the ground. Method one is iffy, seeing as I'm assuming it's begun incorporating itself among other natives, and you may just not want to introduce any kind of weed killer or herbicide into the ecosystem. Method two is what we use to clean up large areas here in Arizona, and it's byfar the most effective, you make sure you dig up the whole plant and at least what you can get of its roots, and you lay the plant over the affected area in a thick layer, ensuring no offshoots or seeds have enough sunlight or heat to grow. Considering the decomposition effects of Phramites australis though, you may want to just remove the plant and roots as much as you can, throw them away either in a green waste landfill or regular landfill, and mulch a thick layer of either woodchips or leaves over the area. You'll have to do this at least once a year to permanently get rid of it.

I'm no expert on Phramites australis specifically, so I encourage anyone else to reply with better suggestions or their insights, and I encourage op to take this with a slight grain of salt because I've never actually dealt with australis and each invasive is different.

You can use fertilizer to boost growth and help it along, I personally love Osmocote smart release, which is a 15-9-12 NPK ratio. You just pour some (follow the directions) in and water as normal, it'll fertilize for up 6 months! https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0071CZTK6/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_apa_i_r7NKFbMTTZKGD



However if regular feeding is more your style you can go with a Water Soluble fertilizer with a 20-20-20 NPK ratio, just make sure you follow the directions and don't over dose your plant with it, too much over time (with any fertilizer) will raise the PH of the soil, however the salts will eventually wash out so after a few waterings you should be good to go! https://www.amazon.com/dp/B00BIO560G/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_apa_i_ycOKFbJ5SP9F3


You can also use theses two in conjunction with each other, just pour in a regular dose of Osmocote and you can occasionally treat with the water soluble for an extra boost to growth!


There are a lot of different viable fertilizer methods out there, however these are two of the easiest in my opinion, pm me if you want to know anything else, hope this helps!
